knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

# Part A - Creating Matrices

```{r}
# Create m1
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1
```

```{r}
# Create m2 using byrow = TRUE
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
```

```{r}
# Create scores matrix
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90),
                 nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

# Print scores
scores
```

 Question 1

```{r}
# Answer:
# m1 fills the numbers column by column, while m2 fills the numbers row by row.
# byrow = TRUE tells R to fill the matrix horizontally first before moving to the next row.
```

 Question 2

```{r}
# Test with only 8 numbers
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)

# R repeats the numbers to fill the missing slot in the matrix. It also gives a warning because 8 numbers cannot be evenly arranged into 9 slots
```

# Part B - Subsetting Matrices

```{r}
# Get row 1, column 2
scores[1, 2]
```

```{r}
# Get the entire first row
scores[1, ]
```

```{r}
# Get the entire Ben column
scores[, "Ben"]
```

```{r}
# Get scores that are greater than or equal to 90
scores[scores >= 90]
```

 Question 3

```{r}
# Check the class of a row and a column
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])

# R automatically changes a single row or column into a vector.It does this because a vector is simpler to use when the result contains only one dimension.
```

 Question 4

```{r}
# Logical subsetting returns only the values that satisfy the condition.
# It does not keep the original rows and columns, so the 2D shape and names are removed.
```

# Part C - Matrix Properties and Operations

```{r}
# Check the dimensions of scores
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)
```

```{r}
# Transpose scores
scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t

# Compare dimensions
dim(scores)
dim(scores_t)
```

```{r}
# Create matrices a and b
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)

# Addition
a + b

# Element-wise multiplication
a * b
```

```{r}
# True matrix multiplication
a %*% b
```

 Question 5

```{r}
# Element-wise multiplication multiplies the numbers in the same positions. Matrix multiplication uses rows from the first matrix and columns from the second matrix to calculate new values.
```

 Question 6

```{r}
# The row names become column names, and the column names become row names.
# They swap because the rows and columns switch positions when a matrix is transposed.
```

# Part D - cbind() and rbind()

```{r}
# Add Dex as a new column
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2
```

```{r}
# Add Quiz3 as a new row to the original scores
scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```

 Question 7

```{r}
# Test cbind with 3 values
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))

# R will recycle the values to fit the number of rows and give a warning because 3 values do not match the 2 rows of scores. cbind and rbind work best when the dimensions match correctly.
```

 Question 8

```{r}
# Answer:
# I would use rbind when adding new observations or rows to a dataset.
# For example, if I record daily sales, I can add each new day as another row
# because the new data has the same columns as the existing dataset.
```

# Part E - Arrays: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
# Create a 2x3x2 array
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr
```

```{r}
# Access row 1, column 2, of the second layer
arr[1, 2, 2]
```

```{r}
# Get the entire first layer
arr[, , 1]
```

```{r}
# Confirm the dimensions
dim(arr)
```

 Question 9

```{r}
# The first number represents the rows, the second represents the columns,
# and the third represents the layers of the array.
# Our array has 2 rows, 3 columns, and 2 layers.
```

Question 10

```{r}
# An example is monthly sales of different products in different stores.
# Rows can represent stores, columns can represent products, and the third dimension
# can represent months. A matrix is not enough because it can only store two dimensions at a time.
```

# Part F - Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
# Create class matrices
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

# Combine new students using rbind()
all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students
```

```{r}
# Compute the average score of each student
rowMeans(all_students)
```

Question 11

```{r}
# I chose rbind because class_b contains new students, so they need to be added as new rows.
# Both matrices have the same column names, Midterm and Final, which means their columns match.
```

 Question 12

```{r}
# I would use rbind to combine the five class matrices because each class has the same columns.After combining them, I would use dim() to check if the total number of rows equals all students from the five classes and if there are still 2 columns for Midterm and Final.
```
